Kazimir Malevich, the Ukrainian-Russian avant-garde artist and theorist who created Suprematism, one of modernism's most radical movements.

In nineteen fifteen, Malevich created the Black Square, a simple black square on white ground. The work shocked and baffled the art world, and it remains the symbol of radical abstraction. He positioned it above a door in his studio like an icon—a spiritual gesture. Some see it as the ultimate negation of art; others see it as the purest affirmation of painting's essence.

Malevich developed Suprematism, the belief that supremacy lies in pure feeling, expressed through geometric abstraction alone. He moved through Cubism and Futurism before reaching abstraction, each style more radical than the last. His later geometric paintings explore endless variations of colored rectangles, striving for what he called pure feeling. He saw Suprematism as a complete break from representation—not modernism, but a new artistic system rooted in pure sensation and zero-objectivity.

In nineteen twenty-seven, Malevich coined the term Suprematism and published The Non-Objective World, his theoretical manifesto. Like many Soviet artists, though, he faced suppression under Stalin. His radical abstraction was denounced as formalist and bourgeois. His work was hidden and nearly destroyed. Under Soviet rule, Malevich worked quietly, developing a practice that would not be fully understood or appreciated until decades after his death.
